content: Queen Alexandra's Royal Naval Nursing Service (QARNNS) is the dedicated nursing branch of the British Royal Navy. Its personnel collaborate closely with the Royal Navy Medical Branch. As of January 1, 2006, the service comprised 240 Naval Nurses and 90 Nursing Officers, as reported by Don Touhig, a former junior minister of the Ministry of Defence. In 1883, a committee identified the need for improvements in medical and nursing care within the Royal Navy. Consequently, in 1884, a uniformed Naval Nursing Service was established, staffed by professionally trained nurses. These nurses initially served at shore-based facilities in Haslar and Plymouth. In 1902, Queen Alexandra, the consort of King Edward VII, became the President of the Nursing Staff. In her honor, the service was renamed Queen Alexandra's Royal Naval Nursing Service. A reserve branch, the Queen Alexandra's Royal Naval Nursing Service Reserve, was created on October 13, 1910. During the First World War in 1914, QARNNS expanded significantly, incorporating numerous volunteers from the British Red Cross and civilian hospitals. Similarly, during the Second World War, many volunteer nurses from QARNNS were deployed to overseas locations. In 1949, a nursing branch was formed within the Women's Royal Naval Service (WRNS), but by 1960, these nurses were integrated into QARNNS, unifying the nursing services. In 1982, the service became inclusive of male nurses, and the first male officer, Senior Nursing Officer Rajendrasen Purusrum, was commissioned on March 1, 1983. Although QARNNS was fully affiliated with the Royal Navy from 1977, it remained technically a separate entity until March 31, 2000, when it officially became part of the Royal Navy. Queen Alexandra served as President of the service until her death in 1925, after which Queen Mary succeeded her in 1926. Princess Alexandra became the Patron of QARNNS in 1955. Initially, the service had only two ranks: Nursing Sister and Head Sister. In 1911, an intermediate rank, Superintending Sister, was introduced. The position of Head Sister-in-Chief, overseeing the entire service, was established on August 1, 1927. By 1937, the titles of Head Sister and Head Sister-in-Chief were changed to Matron and Matron-in-Chief, respectively. During the Second World War, a new ranking system was introduced for Ratings, who were referred to as Naval Nurses. Their ranks were aligned with those of Royal Navy Ratings. In 1982, the ranking system for Nursing Officers was revised to accommodate the inclusion of male officers. By 1995, QARNNS adopted the standard Royal Navy ranking system.
